answers.reasoning: The pole-zero matching method maps continuous-time poles at s = a_i to discrete-time poles at z = e^{a_i T_s} and continuous-time zeros at s = b_i to discrete-time zeros at z = e^{b_i T_s}. Stability in continuous-time (all poles in LHP) does not guarantee stability in discrete-time under this method. For example, a continuous-time stable system with a pole on the imaginary axis may become unstable in discrete-time due to the mapping of that pole to a discrete-time pole off the unit circle. Similarly, an unstable continuous-time system will generally remain unstable in discrete-time under this method. Therefore, options A, B, D, and F are incorrect. Option C states that none of the other statements is correct, which is true because A, B, D, and F are all false.

The given transfer function is H(s) = \(\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{M}(s - b_i)}{\prod_{i=1}^{N}(s - a_i)}\). For a continuous-time LTI system to be causal, all poles must lie in the left half of the complex plane (i.e., Re(a_i) < 0 for all i). When discretized via pole-zero matching with sampling time T_s, the poles of the discrete-time system are p_i = e^{a_i T_s} and zeros are z_i = e^{b_i T_s}. If the original CT system is causal (all a_i are in the left half-plane), then all p_i = e^{a_i T_s} will also lie in the left half-plane (since the exponential of a negative real number remains negative real), making the discrete-time system causal as well. Conversely, if the CT system is non-causal (some a_i have non-negative real parts), then some p_i will lie in the right half-plane or on the imaginary axis, making the discrete-time system non-causal. Therefore, causality is preserved under this discretization method. This eliminates options A, D, and F. Option B claims the discretized system is always causal, which is not true if the original CT system is non-causal. Hence, the correct statement is that if the CT system is causal, then the discretized system is causal.

The pole-zero matching method maps the continuous-time poles at s = a_i to discrete-time poles at z = e^{a_i T_s} and zeros at s = b_i to z = e^{b_i T_s}. The relationship between the continuous-time frequency ω and discrete-time frequency Ω is given by Ω = (2π / T_s) * ln(s / a_i) evaluated at s = jω, which becomes Ω = (2π / T_s) * ln(jω / a_i). This logarithmic relationship means that the mapping of the jω axis in the s-plane to the unit circle in the z-plane is not a simple one-to-one wrapping but rather a warped mapping. Specifically, the jω axis is wrapped around the unit circle in the z-plane, but due to the logarithmic nature of the mapping, it wraps around the unit circle once as ω varies from 0 to ∞. Therefore, option A correctly describes the transformation, while options B, C, and D are incorrect.

The DC gain of a continuous-time transfer function H(s) is found by evaluating H(s) at s = 0. For H(s) = 1/(s + 1), the DC gain is H(0) = 1/(0 + 1) = 1. The discrete-time transfer function W(z) is given by W(z) = k_d / (z + e^{-T_s}). The DC gain of a discrete-time system is found by evaluating W(z) at z = 1 (since z = e^{jωT_s}, at ω = 0, z = 1). So, DC gain of W(z) is W(1) = k_d / (1 + e^{-T_s}). We need this to equal the DC gain of H(s), which is 1. Therefore, k_d / (1 + e^{-T_s}) = 1 => k_d = 1 + e^{-T_s}.
